articles.title: Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri becomes Morocco’s first woman prime minister
articles.summary:
Image alt text: Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri speaks at a televised address after being appointed Morocco’s first woman prime minister On September 29, King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as Morocco’s prime minister, making the 50-year-old urban planner and longtime mayor of Marrakesh the first woman to hold the role in the kingdom’s […]
The post Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri becomes Morocco’s first woman prime minister first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
Image alt text: Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri speaks at a televised address after being appointed Morocco’s first woman prime minister

On September 29, King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as Morocco’s prime minister, making the 50-year-old urban planner and longtime mayor of Marrakesh the first woman to hold the role in the kingdom’s history. She is also the third woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world. “For the first time in our country’s history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government,” El Mansouri said in a televised address. “This is a source of pride not only for me but for all Moroccan women.”

From Marrakesh’s city hall to the prime minister’s office

El Mansouri was born in Marrakesh in 1976 and studied law, earning a diploma in advanced studies from the University of Montpellier in France and a diploma in Anglo-Saxon business law from New York University. She entered local politics in 2009, elected mayor of Marrakesh at 33 and the first woman to hold that office. After the 2021 elections she returned to lead the Marrakesh municipal council and served multiple terms in the House of Representatives.

In October 2021 she moved into national government as Minister of National Spatial Planning, Urban Development, Housing and Urban Policy. That put her in charge of housing reform and, more urgently, the effort to rehouse tens of thousands of people displaced by the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake, which killed nearly 3,000 people and wiped out whole villages in the High Atlas mountains.

Building a coalition with the World Cup on the clock

El Mansouri’s Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won the most seats in Morocco’s September elections, taking 97 of the 395 seats in the House of Representatives. That’s well short of the 198 needed for a majority, so building a coalition comes first. The Justice and Development Party and the Federation of Democratic Left have both announced they’re staying in opposition. PAM, founded in 2008 and closely tied to the monarchy, has said it will work with anyone else.

The government she puts together will be running things during Morocco’s build-up to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, co-hosted with Portugal and Spain, with billions in infrastructure spending attached and a level of international attention that tends to raise the stakes on everything. El Mansouri spent her career in urban planning, housing reform, and post-earthquake rebuilding. Given what’s coming, that’s not an accidental fit.

The third woman prime minister in the Arab world

El Mansouri follows two Tunisian predecessors: Najla Bouden, who served from October 2021 to August 2023, and Sara Zaafarani, appointed in March 2025 and still in the role. Ten years ago the idea of three women holding prime ministerial office across two Arab countries in five years would have seemed optimistic. Morocco has also seen women’s parliamentary representation grow steadily over the same period.

Now she has to hold a coalition together, run a budget, and deliver on the housing and urban development agenda she has been carrying since 2021. The World Cup investment will reshape Moroccan cities long after the final whistle, and whoever oversees that money will have a lot to answer for. She called the appointment “truly historic.” On that score she’s probably right. Whether her government earns the same description is a different question.

articles.title: Digital hopes, real power: From connection to collective action
articles.summary: If the Arab Spring was defined by optimism about what the internet could do, the years since have been marked by a more sober understanding of what it takes to defend it
articles.content:
This article was originally published by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) on April 30, 2026, and an edited version is republished here with permission. It is also part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Back in 2011, the term “digital rights” was still fairly new. In the decades prior, open source and hacker communities, as well as a handful of organizations, had advocated for digital freedoms. It was through the merging of disparate communities from around the world in the 2000s that digital rights came to be more clearly understood as an extension of fundamental human rights.

In 2011, we observed that there were only a few organizations focused on digital rights in the region. Groups like Nawaat, which emerged from the Tunisian diaspora under the Ben Ali regime; the Arab Digital Expression Foundation, formed to promote the creative use of technology; and SMEX, which was initially created to teach journalists and others about social media but has grown to become a powerful force in the region, led the way.

Since then, dozens of organizations have emerged throughout the region to promote freedom of expression, innovation, privacy, and digital security.

Understanding how the digital rights movement evolved in West Asia and North Africa requires a closer look at the communities that shaped it, and the organizations that are carrying on the fight today. Perspectives from people and organizations that were key to these efforts offer critical insight into how the movement has grown and what challenges lie ahead.

Reem Almasri, a senior researcher and digital sovereignty consultant, says that:

‘Digital rights’ emerged as a term around the Arab Spring, when the internet was still a fairly unregulated space, we were still trying to figure out the tech companies’ policies, and force governments to look at the internet as a fundamental right like water and electricity. But then the need to converge digital rights to everyday rights—economic, political, social rights—and to connect it to geopolitics has started to be thought about, and to be in discussion as well. And to not look at digital rights as a separate field from everything else that’s affecting it, from the geopolitical context.

Mohamad Najem, who co-founded SMEX in 2008 and has led it to become the largest organization in the region, told me that, at the time, “Nobody gave [social media] a lot of attention in our region.” Their work was “a positive approach to social media, how we can democratize sharing information, how we can share more from civil society, change people’s minds, et cetera.”

“After that phase,” he continues, “we can think about 2012–2013 — after the Arab Spring, as an organization we started looking at the infrastructure of the internet, and how freedom of expression and privacy are affected. That’s when we started looking more at what we call digital rights.”

Towards tech accountability

In the aftermath of the Arab Spring, social media companies moved from a largely hands-off approach to governance toward more formalized — and often opaque — content moderation systems. Platforms expanded their trust and safety teams and began working more closely with civil society through trusted partnerships in the region and globally. But Najem says:

After the expansion of tech accountability itself and the adaptation of tech companies, we’ve noticed that it’s not taking us anywhere. Gradually we’ve come to a new phase where it feels like tech accountability is an economy by itself that is not leading to real results. So the next phase for us at least and maybe for others in global majority communities is how we can focus on digital public good, how we can push more governments, private and public institutions to adopt more open source software, to look at the ecosystem and understand the US threats happening now, et cetera.

Another group that has played a key role in the fight for digital rights and tech accountability in the region is 7amleh, a Palestinian organization that was founded in 2013. At the time, says Jalal Abukhater:

[I]t was unique and interesting in Palestinian society to have a human rights organization dedicated fully to the topic of digital rights, you know, human rights in a digital format. However, with the years, we saw various milestones, we saw progress of policy decisions and movements through the Israeli government to influence content moderation in Big Tech companies. We saw problems there as an organization. 7amleh took a leading stance in fighting to preserve the digital rights of Palestinians during a period where there was a very strong influence through the Israeli government. There was actually quite important reporting coming through 7amleh on the situation of online content moderation at a time when it wasn’t really a topic being discussed but it was very clearly a situation where there was major influence by government and political suppression happening as a result.

An ever-expanding ecosystem

While in the early days, the digital rights movement attracted specialists, today, people from other fields have recognized how digital rights intersect with their work, and the digital rights community has embraced them.

Almasri says:

Because the digital rights movement has been decentralizing and has stopped being a speciality, it stopped being an exclusive thing for digital rights specialists, since of course the internet not only in the Arab region but all over the world has become a fundamental infrastructure for running any kind of sensitive operations, or operations in general…all types of organizations, and companies, and initiatives are thinking about their digital security, about how internet laws are affecting the use of the internet, or putting them at risk, and how surveillance technologies are affecting their operations.

Abukhater credits the collaborative work that emerged within the region over the years in building the movement’s strength:

[Today], civil society and digital civil society have many forums, many coalitions and networks, but it’s always important to remember that this is work that builds over many years of experience, and relationships, and networks—that it’s different parties coming to support each other at different phases to ensure that this kind of work succeeds and that this ecosystem is sustained globally with support from partner organizations which were very crucial in ensuring that this ecosystem is sustained, especially in Palestine.

Growing collaborations

Conferences like Bread and Net, first held in Beirut in 2018, and the Palestine Digital Activism Forum (PDAF), first held in Ramallah in 2017, bring activists, academics, journalists, and other practitioners together to network and learn about each other’s work. The pandemic, conflict, and other barriers haven’t stopped either conference from carrying on: PDAF has become an annual virtual event that draws big-name speakers, while Bread & Net has spaced out its meetings but continues to draw bigger crowds each time.

Almasri credits these meetings with expanding the movement beyond the traditional techies and activists who first got involved. “You see a wide spectrum of different fields. You see artists, archivists, journalists joining these conversations, which is definitely on the brighter side of things when it comes to this field, or this scene.”

She also credits the emergence of alliances such as the Middle East Alliance for Digital Rights (MADR, of which EFF is a member), founded in 2020 by individuals and organizations who had been working together for many years to formalize those collaborations.

“Other than the collaborations at the advocacy level, [MADR] creates a sort of pressure point on Big Tech, on content moderation policies, allows for certain coordination at the level of the UN, et cetera, which I see as really positive because it brings some of the redundant efforts together and helps decide on priorities.”

Looking forward

In thinking about the future of the movement, Almasri and Najem agree that digital rights are no longer a niche. In Najem’s words, “It’s about everything else…it’s about everything.”

Almasri adds:

[W]hen it comes to priorities, things that this scene has been working on, I feel that October 7 [2023] was a big turning point in the way that digital rights activists, researchers, and academics—this field—is looking at digital rights in general. Of course, there is the major question of the need to revise tactics to fight Israel’s tech-enabled genocide that is also empowered by the global economy, big tech, and governments of the world? What alliances should we start building on a regional and global level?

She sees “digital sovereignty,” the ability of people and communities to choose, control, and use technology that serves their needs and values, as one of the next big topics for the movement to tackle, as debates over who owns and hosts our data have sharpened amid revelations that U.S. companies have played a role in regional conflicts.

There have been pockets of debates on how to achieve digital sovereignty, especially from human rights organizations documenting war crimes … There’s an awareness of how the dependence on US-based providers, cloud storage, even hosting infrastructure is a risk, especially after how using these services has been weaponized against the digital existence of certain organizations in the region that have been deplatformed or had their content removed on platforms like Meta and YouTube because their content doesn’t align with the foreign policy of the United States…so it raises a big question about how we look at digital independence, what is the spectrum of independence that civil society in the region can achieve, and in relation to what’s available as well.

Almasri also points to the role of researchers in the region:

There has been a lot more research on the political economy of surveillance technologies, so not only looking at how governments are using them, but their supply chain, who’s investing in these technologies, and how geopolitical networks empowered their proliferation in the hands of governments. This is where studies looking at the political economy of AI and the military become important, trying to understand how this field of weapons, the military, and AI grew together as part of this global capitalist system rather than looking at these technologies in silos, that is. Looking at the proliferation of these technologies from a geopolitical point of view, looking at the bigger ecosystem rather than zooming in to the specifics of it. I think this has been a big development in the way that we look at digital rights, and the way that digital rights have been converged and integrated into the geopolitical scene.

As the global digital rights community continues to expand, it’s clear that the questions at its core are no longer just about access or expression, but about power — who holds it, how it is exercised, and who is left out of its protections. What began as a fight to keep the internet open has become a broader effort to reimagine it — an effort that is grappling with questions of infrastructure, ownership, and the global inequalities embedded in both.

And yet, despite the scale of these challenges, the movement’s strength lies in the solidarity, the ecosystems, and the networks it has spent more than a decade building. From the early days of the blogging and techie communities to the increasingly powerful digital rights community, advocates in the region have gone up against dictators, endured war and repression, yet remain determined to push forward.
articles.reasoning: The article details the significant evolution and expansion of the digital rights movement in West Asia and North Africa since the Arab Spring, highlighting how digital rights have become recognized as fundamental human rights. It emphasizes broad societal impact through advocacy for freedom of expression, privacy, and digital sovereignty, with tangible progress in policy and community building. The story focuses on the collective action of multiple organizations and activists, illustrating a meaningful and sustained positive change in digital freedoms and human rights in a geopolitically complex region.
articles.personality_title: How digital rights grew from hope to real action in West Asia and North Africa
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2011, during the Arab Spring, people in West Asia and North Africa began to see the internet as more than just a tool. It became a place where digital rights—like freedom of expression and privacy—were linked to basic human rights. At that time, only a few groups focused on protecting these rights online.

**What happened** – Since then, many organizations have formed to defend digital freedoms. Groups like SMEX and 7amleh have worked to protect online speech and privacy, even when facing political pressure. Activists and experts have built networks, held conferences, and pushed for more open and fair internet rules. They also started focusing on “digital sovereignty,” meaning communities controlling their own technology and data.

**Impact** – This movement has grown from small tech groups to a broad, strong community that includes artists, journalists, and human rights defenders. They have influenced policies and challenged big tech companies to be more accountable. Their work connects digital rights to bigger issues like politics and security, showing how the internet affects many parts of life.

**What's next step** – The movement is now focusing on fighting digital control tied to global politics, especially issues around data ownership and surveillance. Activists want to build stronger regional and global partnerships to protect people’s rights online and promote digital independence from powerful tech companies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Over more than a decade, digital rights advocates in West Asia and North Africa have turned early internet hopes into lasting action that links technology to human rights and political power.

articles.title: Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
articles.summary: A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, suggests that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own evolutionary patterns.
articles.content:
New research from the University of Lincoln, UK, is questioning a long standing idea about the evolutionary roots of human violence. The findings suggest that everyday aggression does not necessarily build toward deadly conflict.

Published in the international journal Evolution Letters, the study indicates that mild aggression and lethal violence may have developed through different evolutionary processes. That distinction adds a new layer to the long-running debate over whether violence is an inherent part of human nature.

The work was led by Professor Bonaventura Majolo of the University of Lincoln, alongside Dr. Samantha Wakes and Professor Marcello Ruta.

Aggression May Not Be a Single Trait

Many theories about the origins of violence treat aggression as one broad behavioral characteristic. Under that view, species that frequently engage in everyday fights or disputes might also be expected to show higher levels of lethal violence.

The new research suggests that this assumption may be too simple.

The team examined patterns of aggression across 100 primate species, including humans. Their analysis showed that species with high levels of mild aggression were not necessarily more likely to kill competitors.

Instead, deadly behaviors such as killing adult rivals or infanticide appeared to follow their own evolutionary patterns, largely separate from routine conflict.

Mild Conflict and Lethal Violence Follow Different Paths

The results challenge the idea that violence can be explained as a straightforward evolutionary inheritance.

Rather than forming a single scale that runs from minor disputes to lethal attacks, different types of aggression may arise under different social and evolutionary pressures.

That suggests the link between everyday aggression and extreme violence could be much weaker than some previous theories have proposed.

Bonaventura Majolo, Professor of Social Evolution, said: "Understanding the evolutionary roots of violence is important not only for biology but also for how we think about human behavior.

"Our study shows that the evolution of aggression follows more complex patterns than what earlier models proposed, that it is biologically inaccurate to rank species on the basis of their general propensity for aggression and that we need a more nuanced approach when discussing whether humans are inherently violent."

What 100 Primate Species Reveal

The researchers compared five different forms of aggression, ranging from ordinary conflicts to lethal attacks, using a large dataset spanning many primate species.

They found that different types of lethal aggression were moderately associated with one another. However, those forms of deadly violence showed little connection with mild aggression.

That pattern suggests that the biological and evolutionary mechanisms behind lethal violence are distinct from those that drive everyday conflict.

The findings add new evidence to a longstanding debate in anthropology and evolutionary biology over what shapes human violence. Researchers have long questioned whether violent behavior is rooted mainly in deep evolutionary history or is more strongly influenced by social and cultural forces.
articles.reasoning: The study challenges the long-held belief that humans are inherently violent by showing that everyday aggression and lethal violence evolved differently. This insight has broad implications for understanding human behavior and promoting a more nuanced, less fatalistic view of violence, which can inspire hope for reducing violence in society.
articles.personality_title: New study shows everyday aggression and deadly violence evolved differently in primates
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wondered if humans are naturally violent or if violence comes from other causes. Many believed that small fights and deadly attacks are part of the same behavior, just different levels of aggression.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of Lincoln studied 100 species of primates, including humans. They looked at different kinds of aggression, from mild fights to killing rivals. Their study, published in Evolution Letters, found that species that often fight are not always the ones that kill others. Instead, lethal violence like killing rivals or babies follows separate evolutionary patterns.

**Impact** – This discovery changes how we think about violence in humans and animals. It shows that everyday arguing or fighting doesn’t automatically lead to deadly violence. This means human violence is more complicated and not just a simple, natural trait. Understanding this can help us think differently about how violence develops and how it might be reduced.

**What's next step** – Scientists will likely explore what specific social or environmental factors cause lethal violence to develop separately from mild aggression. They may also study how this new understanding can help in preventing violence in human communities.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Research reveals that mild aggression and deadly violence in primates, including humans, evolved through different paths, challenging the idea that humans are naturally violent in all forms.

articles.title: In Islamabad, Guterres calls for end to US-Iran conflict
articles.summary: The UN Secretary-General appealed on Tuesday for an end to the United States-Iran war and the toll it has taken on global trade, as he began an official visit to Pakistan.
articles.content:
“From Islamabad, I want to send a loud and clear message to all parties,” António Guterres told journalists in the capital.

“End the conflict. Return to diplomacy. Fully restore navigational rights and freedoms in accordance with international law.”

Regional escalation

The crisis began in late February following joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

In response, Tehran launched counter attacks on targets in Gulf countries and Jordan, and blocked transit through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint.

The maritime corridor is critical for global trade in crude oil, fertilisers and liquified natural gas. Hundreds of ships and their crews have been stuck at sea for months.

Tweet URL

Meanwhile, fighting has spread to Yemen’s Red Sea coast where Iran-backed Houthi forces are battling Government troops, supported by Saudi Arabia, for control of the crucial Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Pakistan’s ‘pivotal role’

The Secretary-General saluted Pakistan for its leadership in helping to create the conditions for dialogue between the US and Iran.

“Your efforts helped deliver the 17 June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, the subsequent ceasefire, and the framework for further negotiations,” he said, adding that “every Pakistani should be proud of that pivotal role.”

Addressing wider issues, Mr. Guterres said that “there will never be peace in the region until the right of self-determination of the Palestinian people is fully realized – as Pakistan has long championed”

He expressed hope for regional peace and prosperity, “anchored in dialogue and cooperation.”

The Secretary-General praised Pakistan for being “a source of solidarity and solutions.”

For decades, the country has sheltered millions of Afghans fleeing conflict and instability, and he underlined UN commitment to work with Pakistan to ensure that returns are voluntary, safe and dignified.

He recalled that Pakistan has served as a member of the UN Security Council over the past two years.

“At a time of growing division and mistrust around the world, Pakistan put a spotlight on the value of multilateralism, dialogue, mediation and diplomacy,” he said.

Mr. Guterres added that Pakistan is also among the world’s longstanding and largest contributors to UN peacekeeping. He paid tribute to the more than 180 Pakistani blue helmets who “gave their lives in the service of peace.”

Pakistan and Denmark also took the lead on UN Security Council resolution 2823, which strengthens accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers.

He noted that 153 countries co-sponsored the document, making it “the largest number of co-sponsors for a Security Council resolution in United Nations history.”

The Secretary-General also acknowledged the “immense suffering” Pakistan has endured due to deadly terrorist attacks.

Mr. Guterres concluded by addressing the climate crisis, recalling that his last visit to Pakistan came during the catastrophic floods in 2022.

Climate action leader

“Pakistan is on the frontlines of climate chaos despite contributing only a tiny fraction of global emissions,” he said, but “it is also on the frontlines of the response.”

He pointed to the country’s leadership in establishing the Loss and Damage Fund, and the growing clean energy transition in the country.

The UN chief used the occasion to again call for developed countries to take the lead in ensuring a “drastic reduction” in global emissions this decade.

articles.personality_title: UN chief urges end to US-Iran conflict, praises Pakistan’s peace efforts

articles.personality_title_fr: Le chef de l’ONU appelle à la fin du conflit États-Unis-Iran et salue les efforts de paix du Pakistan
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les tensions entre les États-Unis et l’Iran ont augmenté depuis février, après des frappes conjointes américano-israéliennes sur l’Iran. Cela a entraîné des contre-attaques iraniennes et un blocus du détroit d’Hormuz, une route clé pour le commerce mondial, affectant de nombreux navires.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Mardi, le secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a visité Islamabad, la capitale du Pakistan, et a appelé à la fin du conflit entre les États-Unis et l’Iran. Il a demandé à toutes les parties d’arrêter les combats, de reprendre les discussions et de respecter les lois internationales sur la liberté de navigation. Guterres a aussi salué le Pakistan pour son rôle dans l’accord de cessez-le-feu signé en juin et pour son soutien aux négociations en cours.

**Impact** – Cette situation est importante car le conflit affecte le commerce mondial et la stabilité régionale. Le rôle du Pakistan dans la promotion du dialogue montre comment les pays peuvent aider à réduire les tensions par la voie pacifique. Le chef de l’ONU a également souligné les efforts du Pakistan pour accueillir les réfugiés afghans, soutenir les opérations de maintien de la paix de l’ONU et agir contre le changement climatique malgré ses propres difficultés.

**Prochaines étapes** – Le cessez-le-feu et le cadre de négociation visent à faire avancer le processus de paix. L’ONU et le Pakistan prévoient de continuer à travailler ensemble pour assurer des retours de réfugiés sûrs et pour renforcer les actions climatiques dans le monde.

**En une phrase** – La visite du secrétaire général de l’ONU met en lumière le rôle clé du Pakistan dans la promotion de la paix entre les États-Unis et l’Iran tout en encourageant la diplomatie et la coopération mondiale sur les réfugiés et le climat.
